div.head: ECf 32 C 3
div.ab: Cepit enim predictus Ina uxorem suam demum Walam nomine, propter quam uocata est Wallia illa terra que quondam uocabatur Cambria. Bigamus enim fuit. Cepit enim cum ista ultima sua uxore Cambriam et Cornubiam et coronam benedictam Britannie, que fuit ultimo Cadualladrio regi Britannie.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 658 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints across the page as an insertion into ECf retr. 32 (32 A–E, pp. 655–660). The dictionary cites it as “ECf 32 C …”, so it is kept with ECf here.

note.seg: Iam non uocabantur Britones, sed Gualenses, uocabulum .. a Guales regina; Galfr. Monm. XII 19 (was Girald Descr. Cambr. 7 ablehnt); dort (c. 18) lässt Cadwalladrus, der letzte Britenkönig, Iny nepotem die Briten regiren. Da in der Quelle Ine’s Frau anders hiess, muss der Londoner Wala zur zweiten Gemahlin Ine’s machen

Iam non uocabantur Britones, sed Gualenses, uocabulum .. a Guales regina; Geoffrey of Monmouth XII 19 (which Gerald, Descr. Cambr. 7, rejects); there (c. 18) Cadwalader, the last king of the Britons, lets Iny nepotem rule the Britons. Since in the source Ine’s wife had another name, the Londoner has to make Wala Ine’s second wife

div.ab: For the aforesaid Ina at last took as his wife one named Wala, after whom that land was called Wales which was once called Cambria. For he was twice married. For with this last wife of his he took Cambria and Cornwall and the blessed crown of Britain, which had belonged last to Cadwaladr, king of Britain.
